description: There is an integer array nums sorted in non-decreasing order (with possible duplicates). nums is rotated at some pivot. Given the array after rotation and a target, return true if target is in nums, or false otherwise.
intuition: This is binary search in a rotated sorted array with duplicates. The main complication is when nums[lo] == nums[mid] - you can't tell which half is sorted. The fix is simple: just increment lo to skip the duplicate. This degrades worst-case to O(n) but average case remains O(log n).
approach: Modified binary search. When duplicates make it impossible to determine which half is sorted (nums[lo] == nums[mid]), increment lo to skip the duplicate. Otherwise, determine which half is sorted and search accordingly.
jsWalkthrough:
Input: nums = [2,5,6,0,0,1,2], target = 0

lo=0, hi=6
mid=3: nums[3]=0 === target=0 -> return true

---
Input: nums = [2,5,6,0,0,1,2], target = 3

lo=0, hi=6
mid=3: nums[3]=0 != 3; nums[0]=2 != nums[3]=0
  nums[0]=2 <= nums[3]=0? No -> right half sorted
  targetInRight: 0<3 and 3<=nums[6]=2? No -> hi=2
lo=0, hi=2: mid=1: nums[1]=5 != 3; nums[0]=2 != 5
  nums[0]=2 <= nums[1]=5? Yes -> left half sorted
  targetInLeft: 2<=3 and 3<5? Yes -> lo=2
lo=2, hi=2: mid=2: nums[2]=6 != 3; nums[2]=6 != 3
  nums[0... wait lo=2 now: nums[2]=6 <= nums[2]=6? Yes
  targetInLeft: 6<=3? No -> lo=3
lo(3) > hi(2) -> return false
explanation:
1. Standard binary search with modifications for rotation and duplicates.
2. If nums[lo] == nums[mid], we cannot determine which side is sorted; skip lo.
3. If left half is sorted (nums[lo] <= nums[mid]), check if target is in that range.
4. If right half is sorted, check if target is in that range.
5. Worst case degrades to O(n) due to duplicates.
hints: This is similar to Search in Rotated Sorted Array but with duplicates.

In that case, just increment lo to skip the duplicate.

phases.label: Compare boundaries and discard at least one index per iteration

timeComplexityBreakdown.note: Duplicates can force lo to advance by only one. When each comparison halves the range it is O(log n), but the guaranteed worst-case bound is O(n).
